I prefer to have daddy long legs in the house. They are way less scary and do a better job of pest control. Long legs spiders are passive hunters and spin webs in strategic locations to catch bugs. Huntsman spiders are active hunters that don't trap, meaning they have to actually ambush or chase down their pray. On top of that, huntsman bites can actually be a problem. They don't have venom that can harm us, but their hypodermic fangs cause a nasty bite.

While there is no concrete evidence that huntsman bites cause infection and necrosis, I was bitten by a badge huntsman on the ankle twice and the tissue got infected, died, and has been scarred for nearly 9 years now. I'd call that some pretty fkn concrete evidence.

Huntsman spiders are not dangerous in anyway to humans. There is no recorded of a human death from their bite and their venom is not considered medically significant to humans or large mammals. They actually predate highly venomous spider species… so realistically they do you a favour. 

I’ve kept & bred huntsman species in the UK and seen them in the wild. They’re a very diverse and interesting species… one of the few species of spiders that can live communally. The only thing that could be classed as ‘scary’ is their size… which is irrelevant when you compare sizes to other animals that live closely to humans without fear mongering. 
If you take the time to research and maintain an open mind you’ll understand that animals are just animals… created in their own way and have a place on this planet as much as you do.

Australia's scariest spider isn't actually deadly. It's the huntsman spider (family Sparassidae), especially the massive Heteropoda venatoria (the "banana spider" or "giant huntsman"), which gets called the most terrifying arachnid on the planet because of its huge size—legs sometimes spanning up to 30 cm (12 inches) across—and its habit of hiding in houses, under rocks, or on vehicles.

Tourists freak out hard when they spot one (classic viral clips of people screaming and fleeing), so it's the No. 1 "scariest spider" in the world for reactions. But here's the secret: huntsman spiders are generally harmless to humans. They don't spin webs, they're aggressive hunters that stalk and pounce, and their venom is mild (comparable to a bee sting or less). In rare cases, a bite might cause some discomfort or swelling for a day or two, but there's no real medical danger, no antivenom needed, and they're not one of Australia's dangerous species (unlike funnel-webs or redbacks). They're basically big, speedy house guests that eat other bugs.

This starts with the usual "this thing is gonna give you nightmares" setup to grab attention, then drops the surprise: "the huntsman is a big sweetheart." It's all clickbait-style hype for views, but the fact is true—huntsmen are badass (fast runners, great mothers, sometimes hitch rides in cars), not killers.

Fun fact bonus: In Australia they're super common and even welcomed by some locals as "roommates" because they keep the insect population in check. If you're ever in Australia and a big one shows up, just use a cup and paper to relocate it outside—no need to panic!

If you want more on actual deadly spiders (funnel-webs have neurotoxic venom that can be life-threatening) or huntsman biology, let me know. Stay safe out there—spiders are fine, just don't step on them!

A few spider venoms are potent enough to be fatal, though deaths are exceptionally rare today due to accessible medical care and antivenom. The world's most dangerous species include:

Australian Funnel-web Spider (Atrax robustus): Found in eastern Australia, their venom contains a neurotoxin that affects the nervous system. The venom is especially dangerous to primates (including humans), and prior to the creation of an antivenom in 1981, they were responsible for 13 deaths.

Brazilian Wandering Spider (Phoneutria nigriventer): Native to Central and South America, these aggressive spiders possess a potent neurotoxin. While they are considered among the most venomous spiders in the world, deaths are highly unusual when antivenom is administered.

Black Widow (Latrodectus mactans): Common throughout North America and other parts of the world, female black widows have venom that attacks the nervous system. Bites can cause intense pain and muscle spasms, but fatal envenomation is exceedingly rare and generally only threatens children or the elderly without treatment.

Chilean Recluse (Loxosceles laeta): Found primarily in South America, their venom causes skin necrosis but can rarely trigger severe systemic failure, leading to red blood cell rupture and kidney damage, which can be fatal.If you are bitten by a venomous spider, seek emergency medical care immediately.
